questions.q: What do `apiVersion` and `kind` together determine in a Kubernetes manifest?
options: Only cosmetic metadata with no functional effect
Which schema the API server validates the YAML against and which controller handles the object
The namespace the object will be created in
The container image to pull
questions.explain: kind:Deployment is only valid under a specific apiVersion (apps/v1). Mismatching them causes the API server to reject the manifest, since it determines the schema and the responsible controller.

questions.q: What is the difference between an object's `spec` and its `status` field?
options: They are two names for the same data
spec is the desired state you declare; status is the actual observed state the cluster reports back
status is written by hand; spec is generated automatically
spec only applies to Pods, status only applies to Deployments
questions.explain: You write spec to declare what you want. Kubernetes populates status to reflect what's actually happening — the controller manager's job is continuously closing the gap between the two.

questions.q: You write `apiVersion: v1` with `kind: Deployment` in a manifest and apply it. What happens?
options: Kubernetes auto-corrects the apiVersion
The API server rejects the manifest, because v1 does not define a Deployment kind
The Deployment is created with reduced features
It works fine, since apiVersion is only cosmetic
questions.explain: apiVersion and kind must match exactly. Deployment only exists under apps/v1; a mismatch means the API server can't find the right schema and rejects the manifest.

questions.q: What command lets you ask the cluster itself which fields are valid for a given object, without searching external docs?
options: kubectl get all
kubectl explain deployment.spec
kubectl delete deployment
kubectl logs deployment
questions.explain: kubectl explain queries the cluster's own API schema to show valid fields for a given object path, which stays accurate even across different Kubernetes versions.

questions.q: Why does Northbridge's platform team keep Kubernetes manifests in Git and apply them with `kubectl apply -f`, rather than running one-off imperative commands against production?
options: Git is required by Kubernetes to run `apply`
A file in Git is reviewable, diffable, and reproducible, while a one-off command leaves no record of what changed or why
Imperative commands like kubectl scale no longer exist
YAML files run faster than equivalent commands
questions.explain: Storing manifests in version control makes changes reviewable and reproducible — reapplying the same file gives an identical result, unlike an untracked manual command.
